# The *Framework*.

She's on the screen and I can tell from the way she's sitting that she's already made up her mind. We've been talking for maybe twenty minutes — her company, her bottlenecks, what she's hoping AI can fix — and then she leans forward and says it: "Can we just build it? I just need this thing built."

I know exactly what she means. She's seen demos. She's read the case studies. She has a clear picture in her head of the tool that's going to solve her problem, and she wants to stop talking about it and start building it. That's not impatience — that's the instinct of someone who has run a business. When you know what you want, you build it.

But I've also watched what happens when you start there. The build does not go well. The requirements shift two weeks in because nobody mapped what the work actually required — so the spec changes, the scope expands, and the thing that was supposed to take three weeks is now in week seven and still not done. Edge cases surface that nobody anticipated because nobody understood the process well enough to anticipate them. The tool gets deployed eventually, in some version of what was originally scoped, and then the team doesn't use it. Not because they're resistant. Because it doesn't fit how the work actually moves. Nobody understood what people do or what outcomes they're driving toward, and you cannot design around a process you haven't mapped.

Technical friction is a remarkably effective stopper. People route around a tool the moment it adds a step that doesn't make sense to them. When there's no shared understanding of what the constraint actually is — no Signal — the friction compounds at every handoff and the tool quietly gets abandoned. When we trace it back, the answer is always the same: we skipped Signal. We assumed we knew what the constraint was. We built against an assumption, not a diagnosis. The foundation was never poured. The walls went up anyway.

I didn't tell her that on the call. I said: let's start at Signal. She said: okay. We did. What she found there surprised her. The constraint she'd been carrying around in her head for six months wasn't the real constraint — it was a symptom of something two steps upstream. If we'd built what she came in asking for, we'd have solved the symptom beautifully and left the actual problem running.

That is the conversation this chapter exists to prevent you from having with yourself.

This is the chapter that maps the rest of the book. The first two chapters named the problem and named the system that solves it; this one shows the shape of the work itself — the order it runs in, the cadence it runs on, and the single unit of work you will use to learn it. The next six chapters each take one stage of that work and go deep. Treat this chapter as the page you flip back to when you forget which word means what.

## The order is the *argument*.

Most AI initiatives skip the diagnosis and start at Build. A tool gets chosen, a vendor gets paid, a pilot gets launched — and around month nine the CEO is sitting in a board meeting trying to explain why the AI line item produced no operational result. The cause is not the tool. The cause is the order.

<!-- TODO: Revise the "tool/vendor/pilot" framing — SMBs don't run pilots, they tinker and hit a ceiling. Most signals start as hunches. The goal is to formalize the hunch and deconstruct the desired outcome into tasks, processes, and direction. May need to flesh out preceding-chapter frameworks. -->

Building before diagnosing is the same mistake as framing a house before pouring the foundation. The walls go up. The roof goes on. It looks like progress right up until the moment the structure has to carry weight — and then it does not. Construction has rules about the order of operations because the order is load-bearing. So does this.

The Framework exists because there is a correct sequence for installing co-intelligence into a company, and that sequence is the entire reason the result compounds instead of evaporating. Skip the first two steps and you are buying a tool. Run all six in order and you are changing how the work is owned. 

The framework you are about to learn was born from the chutes-and-ladders problem I described at the start of this book. The developer left. The knowledge left with him. And the only reason what came next worked is because I solved the problem in a specific order.

That is the argument. Now the vocabulary.

## Four *words*, defined once.

This book uses four words constantly and they are easy to conflate. Each names a different thing. Here is what each one means — and what it does not.

<!-- DIAGRAM: Four-term relationship map — Framework contains Sequence; Sequence runs on a Sprint; Sprints repeat at the Rhythm. Show the nesting/hierarchy of all four terms so readers can hold the vocabulary in one glance. -->
<!-- FORMAT: diagram -->
<!-- PRIORITY: nice-to-have -->

- **Framework** — the whole six-step shape. When we say "the Framework" or "the Compound Framework," we mean the entire system: the order, the stages, the grouping, the cadence, and the unit of work. It is the noun for everything described in this book.
- **Sequence** — the ordered steps inside the Framework: **Signal → Source → Design → Build → Deliver → Compound**. Always all six. Always in that order, because the order is load-bearing — each stage produces something the next stage requires.
- **Rhythm** — the cadence. Running the Framework over and over. Quarterly. The Rhythm is what turns a single sprint into a compounding business outcome — the same way a weekly L10 is what turns a quarterly Rock into a company that actually executes.
- **Sprint** — one pass through the Sequence on one validated constraint. The term comes from software development, where a sprint is a fixed-length work cycle; here it means a focused unit of work with a defined scope, a clear start, and a measurable end. Duration is set in Design — a Sprint can close in days, run for weeks, or stretch across a quarter, depending on what the constraint requires. The Sprint is the unit of work this book describes and the unit of work you will run. You do not "implement the Framework." You run a Sprint, and then you run another one, and the Rhythm is what holds them together.

The reason to be precise here is that the looser versions of these words are exactly how this kind of work fails. "We're running an AI framework" can mean anything. "We are mid-Sprint, in Design, on the quoting-cycle constraint" is a sentence that locates the work in space and time — and tells you what comes next.

## The six *stages*, at a glance.

The Sequence is six stages. Each gets its own chapter. Here is the role of each one — enough to orient you, with the full depth coming in the chapters that follow.

1. **Signal** — you find the one operational constraint worth solving first, and quantify what it costs.
2. **Source** — you map what the work actually requires: the knowledge, the data, the judgment, the context.
3. **Design** — you decide who does what across the Human+AI workforce for this specific constraint.
4. **Build** — you produce the spec and deploy the workflow into the system your team already uses.
5. **Deliver** — you ship it inside the org, train the people whose handoffs change, and measure the result against what Signal said it cost.
6. **Compound** — you capture the learning, update the infrastructure the next Sprint will use, and rank what comes next.

Six stages. One Sprint. Then again.

## Diagnose, then *Execute & Compound*.

The Sequence splits into two halves, and the split is more important than the stages themselves. The first half is **Diagnose**: Signal and Source. The second half is **Execute & Compound**: Design, Build, Deliver, Compound.

<!-- TODO: Add a visual for the Diagnose / Execute & Compound split. -->

A Sprint that gets stuck in Build almost never has a Build problem. It has a Diagnose problem that surfaced late. Going back to Signal is not failure — it is the Framework doing its job, refusing to let undisclosed assumptions hide inside execution.

Diagnose is the work most companies skip. They skip it because it does not look like progress — no deliverable, no demo, nothing to show the board. It looks like talking. It is the part of the work that determines whether everything downstream is solving the right problem against a real map of what the company knows. Skip it and you Build against the wrong constraint, using data you assumed existed — and the result is not a beautiful workflow that misses the mark. It is a disaster that took an entire Sprint to produce.

<!-- DIAGRAM: Sequence split into two labeled halves — DIAGNOSE (Signal, Source) on the left and EXECUTE & COMPOUND (Design, Build, Deliver, Compound) on the right, with a dividing line and brief rationale for each half. -->
<!-- FORMAT: diagram -->
<!-- PRIORITY: must-have -->

Design is downstream work. It depends entirely on what Signal and Source produced — which is why this book places it inside Execute rather than inside Diagnose. Move it earlier and you are designing against nothing: no validated constraint, no knowledge map.

## What you get *inside* the Framework.

The Sequence is self-implementing. The same way *Traction* gives you the EOS operating system as a book — not a consultant dependency — this book gives you the order of operations and the tools to run a Sprint inside your own company. The order is complete. The vocabulary is precise. A motivated leadership team can pick it up and go.

Two additional layers exist inside the Framework that make each Sprint faster and less expensive. They are not required to start; they are the difference between running the Sequence once and running it well the second time, the third time, and every time after that.

The first is **the Compound Bench**. An agent, in this context, is an AI configured to do a specific job — not a general chatbot, but a role with defined inputs, defined outputs, and a clear scope of action. The Bench is six of them, one per stage of the Sequence. They are not the agents you will deploy inside your company. They are the agents that run the Sequence *with* you — diagnosing, producing, and pressing you to answer the question each stage requires before you move on. Each stage chapter introduces its Bench agent at the moment it does its work. The Bench is available through Compound membership.

The second is **the Skills Library**. A skill, in this context, is a pre-built, installable instrument — a configured piece of workflow logic you port into your own AI stack rather than building from scratch. The Library holds twelve of them, two per stage, and they are the durable artifact. Where the Bench coaches you through a Sprint, the skills stay inside your systems after the Sprint ends, making the next one faster and the one after that faster still. Each stage chapter introduces the relevant pair as the stage is taught. The Library is also available through Compound membership.

<!-- DIAGRAM: Three-layer stack — Framework (base, self-run), Bench (middle, one-per-stage coaching agents), Skills Library (top, installable instruments). Show which layers are included with Compound membership vs. self-service. -->
<!-- FORMAT: diagram -->
<!-- PRIORITY: nice-to-have -->

The shorthand worth holding in your head: the Framework is yours to run. The Bench and Library accelerate it.

## You learn this on a *Sprint*.

You do not learn the Framework by reading about it. You learn it by running one Sprint on one real constraint in your own company. That is the only teaching unit that works, because the Framework is not a model of how AI implementation could go — it is the structure of how the work moves when it moves correctly.

The project coordinator story — the one where we mapped the work instead of posting a job — walks all six stages of the Framework in sequence. You will see it in full in Chapter 6. What it proves here is specific: not that the Sequence is theoretically sound, but that each stage produces something the next stage requires. Signal named the constraint. Source mapped what the role actually required. Design allocated the work between human and agent. Build produced the workflow. Deliver shipped it into the team's environment. Compound captured what the next Sprint would inherit. Remove any one of those steps and the chain breaks. One constraint. Six stages. One documented outcome.

The Sprint is bounded by scope, not by a fixed calendar. One validated constraint, one designed workflow, one measurable result against the cost Signal quantified — Design sets the actual duration, which can be days, weeks, or a quarter depending on what the constraint requires. The narrowness is the discipline that prevents the failure mode every operator has seen: an AI project becoming a platform project, a platform project becoming a reorg, and eighteen months later nothing has shipped. One constraint, one documented outcome. That is the bar.

The Rhythm is what turns that one Sprint into a compounding business. Quarterly, you run another one. The Hybrid Accountability Chart gets one more entry. The knowledge maps get richer. The team's design judgment improves. The Sprints themselves get cheaper and faster, because the infrastructure each Sprint leaves behind accelerates the next one. *Co-Intelligence + Rhythm = Compound.* The Equation is not a slogan — it is a description of what happens to a company that runs this work on a cadence.

The first Sprint is where the Framework stops being something you read about and starts being something your organization can do. Every Sprint after that is what makes the change permanent.

## Begin at *Signal*.

Every Sprint begins in the same place. Before Source can map anything, before Design can allocate anything, before Build can specify anything — Signal has to name the one constraint this Sprint will solve. The discipline of refusing to move forward until that constraint is named, quantified, and validated is the single most important habit the Framework teaches. Most companies will not do it. The ones that do are the ones that compound.
